When these boy bands and girl groups for.New Kids on the Block: This Boston group pioneered the modern boy-band formula in the 1980s, selling tens of millions of records before reuniting in the 2000s.
When these boy bands and girl groups for.Take That: Gary Barlow's band from Manchester had a string of number-one hits, and Robbie Williams left in 1995 for a hugely successful solo career.
When these boy bands and girl groups for.Backstreet Boys: This Florida group became one of the best-selling groups ever, and Millennium alone sold millions of copies during its first weeks.
When these boy bands and girl groups for.Spice Girls: With Girl Power as their slogan, these five women were the best-selling girl group in history, led by Scary, Sporty, Baby, Ginger and Posh.
When these boy bands and girl groups for.NSYNC: Justin Timberlake rose to fame in this group, whose name comes from the last letter of each member's first name.
When these boy bands and girl groups for.Westlife: Irish boy band known for its soaring ballads, who scored a record-setting string of seven consecutive UK number-ones to begin their career.
When these boy bands and girl groups for.Girls Aloud: This British group was formed on a TV talent show, Popstars: The Rivals, and went on to score many UK hits.
When these boy bands and girl groups for.Jonas Brothers: Three brothers from New Jersey who started on Disney Channel, they later returned to the stage after a split in 2013.
When these boy bands and girl groups for.One Direction: The group was assembled on The X Factor and became the first British act to have their first four albums debut at number one in the US.
When these boy bands and girl groups for.Little Mix: Winners of The X Factor in 2011, they were the first group to win the show and later became one of Britain's biggest girl groups.

How fast these spin.Vinyl LP album: Albums were originally slow records for classical music, and 33⅓ rpm was chosen so one side could hold around 20 minutes of sound.
How fast these spin.7-inch vinyl single: This smaller disc, introduced by RCA in 1949, helped make the jukebox a cultural icon of the 1950s and 60s.
How fast these spin.1920s shellac record: These brittle discs, made partly from beetle secretions, held only about three to five minutes per side, so songs were kept short.
How fast these spin.Ceiling fan on high: Fans turn slower than most household machines because the blades are large, and they must move air without making too much noise.
How fast these spin.Car engine at idle: A car engine's idle is its lowest steady speed, while most engines can spin to around 6,000 rpm or higher.
How fast these spin.Washing machine spin: Washing machines spin clothes hard to push water out through the drum holes, spinning at many times the speed of the wash cycle.
How fast these spin.Laptop hard drive: Laptop drives used slower platters to save power and heat, compared with the faster spinning ones in desktop machines.
How fast these spin.Desktop hard drive: Desktop hard drives spin quickly so the read head can reach any bit of data fast, though SSDs have now mostly replaced them.
How fast these spin.Kitchen blender: Blender blades spin extremely fast, easily pulverising ice and tough vegetables, which is why a closed lid is essential.
How fast these spin.Dentist's drill: Air-driven dental handpieces spin at remarkable speeds, which is why modern drills feel much quicker and gentler than the old belt-driven ones.

When these British coins and notes arriv.50p coin: This seven-sided coin was introduced ahead of decimalisation, and its shape was chosen to help people tell it apart.
When these British coins and notes arriv.Decimal penny: Britain switched from pounds, shillings and pence to a 100-penny pound in February 1971, known as Decimal Day.
When these British coins and notes arriv.20p coin: The 20p coin was added to help fill the gap between the 10p and 50p, and it has seven sides like the 50p.
When these British coins and notes arriv.Round £1 coin: The round pound replaced the old pound note, which had been used for almost 170 years, and later became too easy to forge.
When these British coins and notes arriv.£2 coin: A bimetallic coin with a gold-coloured ring around a silver-coloured centre, one of the first to use two metals in circulation.
When these British coins and notes arriv.Polymer £5 note: The first polymer note in the UK featured Winston Churchill, and it is more durable and harder to counterfeit than paper.
When these British coins and notes arriv.12-sided £1 coin: Replacing the round pound, this new coin has twelve sides and a hidden security feature, a hologram-like image.
When these British coins and notes arriv.Polymer £20 note: This polymer note shows J. M. W. Turner and was designed to last longer than paper money.
When these British coins and notes arriv.Polymer £50 note: The last of the polymer notes shows Alan Turing, the codebreaker and computing pioneer.
When these British coins and notes arriv.King Charles III banknotes: The new notes feature the monarch, which was a major change for Britain's currency after decades of the late Queen.

Last of their kind: the year they died.Last aurochs cow: The wild ancestor of domestic cattle, the last known one died in the Jaktorów forest in Poland.
Last of their kind: the year they died.Martha (passenger pigeon): She died at the Cincinnati Zoo on 1 September 1914, and passenger pigeons had once numbered in the billions.
Last of their kind: the year they died.Incas (Carolina parakeet): He died in the same Cincinnati Zoo cage where Martha, the last passenger pigeon, had lived four years earlier.
Last of their kind: the year they died.Booming Ben (heath hen): The last heath hen lived on Martha's Vineyard, and his booming mating call was recorded.
Last of their kind: the year they died.Benjamin (thylacine): The last known thylacine died at Hobart Zoo, and 7 September is Australia's Threatened Species Day.
Last of their kind: the year they died.Turgi (Partula snail): The last known Partula snail of his species, he died at London Zoo, and these snails were wiped out by an introduced predatory snail.
Last of their kind: the year they died.Celia (Pyrenean ibex): The last Pyrenean ibex was found dead under a fallen tree, then cloned in 2003, though the clone lived only minutes.
Last of their kind: the year they died.Lonesome George (tortoise): The last Pinta Island tortoise was found in 1971 and lived at the Galápagos, becoming a conservation symbol, until he died around age 100.
Last of their kind: the year they died.Toughie (Rabbs' tree frog): The last known Rabbs' fringe-limbed tree frog lived at the Atlanta Botanical Garden, and his calls were recorded.
Last of their kind: the year they died.Sudan (northern white rhino): The last male northern white rhino died in Kenya, and only two females remain, so scientists rely on stored embryos.

First flights of famous military jets an.Messerschmitt Bf 109: Nearly 30,000 of them were built, more than any other fighter plane in history.
First flights of famous military jets an.Supermarine Spitfire: Reginald Mitchell's elliptical wing gave it a graceful look, and he died in 1937 before the Battle of Britain made it famous.
First flights of famous military jets an.P-51 Mustang: It underperformed with its original engine until it got a Rolls-Royce Merlin, after which drop tanks let it escort bombers deep into Germany.
First flights of famous military jets an.F-86 Sabre: The first American fighter with swept wings, it battled MiG-15s over Korea in the area known as MiG Alley.
First flights of famous military jets an.MiG-21: Over 10,000 were built, and dozens of air forces have flown it.
First flights of famous military jets an.F-4 Phantom II: Nearly 5,000 were built for the Navy, Air Force and Marines, and early ones carried no gun.
First flights of famous military jets an.F-14 Tomcat: It starred in Top Gun, and variable-sweep wings changed shape in flight; the US Navy retired it in 2006.
First flights of famous military jets an.F-16 Fighting Falcon: Nicknamed the Viper, it was the first production fighter built to be aerodynamically unstable and steered by computers.
First flights of famous military jets an.B-2 Spirit: Only 21 were built, and each cost over a billion dollars, making it among the most expensive aircraft ever.
First flights of famous military jets an.F-35 Lightning II: Lockheed Martin's stealth fighter, with a vertical-takeoff variant, is the most costly weapons program in history.

Voltages from nerves to lightning.Resting nerve cell: Neurons keep about -70 millivolts across their membrane by pumping ions; a nerve signal is a brief flip of that voltage.
Voltages from nerves to lightning.AA battery: This is the standard alkaline size, which is also what AAA, C and D cells deliver, whatever their physical size.
Voltages from nerves to lightning.Coin-cell watch battery: Lithium coin cells like the CR2032 deliver 3 V and are dangerous if swallowed, because they can burn the throat within hours.
Voltages from nerves to lightning.Smoke-alarm battery: Touching its two terminals to your tongue gives a tingle, a famous trick for testing it, though it is not recommended.
Voltages from nerves to lightning.Car battery: It holds six lead-acid cells of about 2.1 volts each, giving the roughly 12 V that starts your engine.
Voltages from nerves to lightning.US wall outlet: North American sockets supply this at 60 Hz, while much of the rest of the world uses roughly double the voltage.
Voltages from nerves to lightning.European wall outlet: At 230 V and 50 Hz, Europe harmonised its supply in the 1990s, replacing a mix of older national standards.
Voltages from nerves to lightning.Electric eel jolt: It is not a true eel but a South American knifefish, and its jolt can stun prey and deter predators.
Voltages from nerves to lightning.Long-distance power line: Transmission lines run at hundreds of thousands of volts because higher voltage means less energy lost as heat over long distances.
Voltages from nerves to lightning.Lightning bolt: A bolt carries roughly 30,000 amps and heats the air around it to about 30,000 degrees Celsius, hotter than the Sun's surface.

Everyday things by thickness.Aluminium foil: Household foil is only about 16 micrometres thick, and it is shiny on one side because two layers are rolled together.
Everyday things by thickness.Printer paper: Standard 80 gsm paper is about 0.1 mm thick; 500 sheets make a ream about 5 cm tall.
Everyday things by thickness.Credit card: ISO 7810 sets its size at 85.6 by 54 by 0.76 mm, which is why cards fit wallets and machines worldwide.
Everyday things by thickness.CD: A CD is 1.2 mm thick, with the data stored in a layer far thinner than a hair.
Everyday things by thickness.US quarter: Its 119 grooved edge ridges, called reeding, originally thwarted people from shaving the silver off coins.
Everyday things by thickness.Smartphone: Modern phones are about 8 mm thick; the original iPhone was 11.6 mm.
Everyday things by thickness.Hockey puck: Regulation pucks are one inch thick, three inches wide and made of vulcanised rubber; they are frozen before games.
Everyday things by thickness.UK house brick: A UK standard brick measures 215 by 102.5 by 65 mm, sized so a bricklayer can hold it in one hand.
Everyday things by thickness.Interior stud wall: Plasterboard on studs leaves a hollow wall, which is why heavy shelves need special fixings.
Everyday things by thickness.Mattress: We spend about a third of life on one, so its thickness matters more than most things on this list.

When these video games were released.Pong: Atari's Pong was based on tennis, and Nolan Bushnell had Allan Alcorn build it as a practice project.
When these video games were released.Space Invaders: It reportedly caused a coin shortage in Japan in 1978.
When these video games were released.Pac-Man: Toru Iwatani reportedly got the idea from a pizza with a slice missing.
When these video games were released.Tetris: Alexey Pajitnov created it in Moscow in 1984; the name merges tetra and tennis.
It rescued the industry after the 1983 crash, and Mario was originally called Jumpman.
When these video games were released.Sonic the Hedgehog: Sega's blue hedgehog was created to rival Mario, and the game is about speed.
When these video games were released.Doom: id Software's 1993 shooter was distributed as shareware, and it popularised online multiplayer deathmatch.
When these video games were released.Pokémon Red and Green: Satoshi Tajiri's game released in Japan in 1996; Red and Blue came to the West.
When these video games were released.World of Warcraft: At its peak it had over 12 million subscribers.
When these video games were released.Fortnite: The battle royale mode launched in 2017 for free and drew hundreds of millions of players.

Computer games by release year.Spacewar!: MIT students made it on a PDP-1 computer, a two-ship duel around a star, among the earliest computer games.
Computer games by release year.Pong: Atari engineer Al Alcorn built it as a training exercise, but the game was so addictive that Atari shipped it.
Computer games by release year.Space Invaders: Its aliens speed up as their numbers shrink, a quirk of limited processing power that became a clever design feature.
Computer games by release year.Pac-Man: Toru Iwatani designed it, and it was originally called Puck-Man in Japan before being changed in the West.
Computer games by release year.Tetris: Alexey Pajitnov made it in Moscow, and its Game Boy version in 1989 sold millions.
Computer games by release year.Doom: Id Software gave away the first episode as shareware, and fans have since made it run on everything from calculators to pregnancy tests.
Computer games by release year.Half-Life: Valve's debut had you start with a tram ride, and its silent hero is physicist Gordon Freeman.
Computer games by release year.The Sims: Will Wright, who also made SimCity, designed it; the characters speak a made-up language called Simlish.
Computer games by release year.Portal: It grew from a student project, Narbacular Drop, and gave the internet the line 'The cake is a lie'.
Computer games by release year.Fortnite: Epic added a free battle royale mode in 2017 and it became a phenomenon, with a world cup in 2019.

Stephen Sondheim musicals, by premiere.A Funny Thing... the Forum: A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum was Sondheim's first show as both composer and lyricist, a farce drawing on the Roman playwright Plautus.
Stephen Sondheim musicals, by premiere.Company: Company is a concept musical about a single man at his 35th birthday, and its ensemble of married friends reflected modern New York.
Stephen Sondheim musicals, by premiere.Follies: Follies reunites showgirls in a theater about to be demolished, and its sumptuous setting remains one of Broadway's costliest productions.
Stephen Sondheim musicals, by premiere.A Little Night Music: A Little Night Music is based on an Ingmar Bergman film and is written largely in waltz time, including the hit 'Send in the Clowns'.
Stephen Sondheim musicals, by premiere.Sweeney Todd: Sweeney Todd, a macabre tale of a murderous barber, was famously operatic and won the Tony Award for Best Musical.
Stephen Sondheim musicals, by premiere.Merrily We Roll Along: Merrily We Roll Along tells its story backward and was a notorious flop initially, but later revivals turned it into a beloved show.
Stephen Sondheim musicals, by premiere.Sunday in the Park with George: Sunday in the Park with George imagines the creation of Seurat's pointillist painting and won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama.
Stephen Sondheim musicals, by premiere.Into the Woods: Into the Woods mixes fairy-tale characters such as Cinderella and Little Red Riding Hood and asks what happens after happily ever after.
Stephen Sondheim musicals, by premiere.Assassins: Assassins brings together those who killed or tried to kill American presidents, in a darkly comic carnival setting.
Stephen Sondheim musicals, by premiere.Passion: Passion, based on an Italian film, tells an obsessive love story and won the Tony for Best Score despite its short run.

Popular psychology books, by publication.Freud on slips of the tongue: Freud's book on slips of the tongue gave us the term Freudian slip.
Popular psychology books, by publication.How to Win Friends: Dale Carnegie's classic has sold over 30 million copies.
Popular psychology books, by publication.Man's Search for Meaning: Viktor Frankl, a Holocaust survivor, reportedly wrote it in just nine days.
Popular psychology books, by publication.Games People Play: Eric Berne's book popularized transactional analysis, describing the hidden scripts in everyday social interactions.
Popular psychology books, by publication.The Man Who Mistook His Wife: Oliver Sacks's collection of case studies is named for a patient who could not recognize faces or objects.
Popular psychology books, by publication.Emotional Intelligence: Daniel Goleman's book popularized the idea of emotional intelligence, or EQ.
Popular psychology books, by publication.Outliers: Malcolm Gladwell popularized the 10,000-hour rule, which researcher Anders Ericsson said he had misrepresented.
Popular psychology books, by publication.Thinking, Fast and Slow: Daniel Kahneman, who won the 2002 economics Nobel, describes two thinking systems, one fast and intuitive, one slow and deliberate.
Popular psychology books, by publication.The Body Keeps the Score: Bessel van der Kolk's book on trauma spent years on bestseller lists.
Popular psychology books, by publication.Atomic Habits: James Clear's book on tiny improvements, one percent better each day, has sold over 20 million copies.

From tweet-sized to doorstopper: word co.The 'baby shoes' story: Often attributed to Hemingway: For sale: baby shoes, never worn. No evidence he wrote it.
From tweet-sized to doorstopper: word co.Gettysburg Address: Lincoln spoke for about two minutes, after Edward Everett had talked for roughly two hours.
From tweet-sized to doorstopper: word co.Declaration of Independence: Jefferson wrote the first draft in June 1776, working in a rented room in Philadelphia.
From tweet-sized to doorstopper: word co.US Constitution (original): It has just seven articles and is the oldest and shortest written national constitution still in use among major governments.
From tweet-sized to doorstopper: word co.The Great Gatsby: It sold modestly in Fitzgerald's lifetime, only becoming an American classic after his death.
From tweet-sized to doorstopper: word co.Harry Potter, book one: In the US it was retitled Sorcerer's Stone, because publishers thought philosopher sounded dull.
From tweet-sized to doorstopper: word co.The Hobbit: Tolkien said he began it by scribbling on a blank exam page: In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit.
From tweet-sized to doorstopper: word co.War and Peace: Tolstoy's novel has more than 500 characters across its sweep of Russian society during the Napoleonic wars.
From tweet-sized to doorstopper: word co.King James Bible: Commissioned by James I and published in 1611, it gave English phrases like the skin of my teeth.
From tweet-sized to doorstopper: word co.In Search of Lost Time: Proust's seven-volume work is famous for the madeleine dipped in tea that unleashes a flood of memories.

Computing before the personal computer.Jacquard punch-card loom: Punched cards told hooks which threads to lift, making this loom among the first machines programmed with holes, a model for later computers.
Computing before the personal computer.Babbage's Difference Engine: Charles Babbage designed it to calculate tables without human error; the Science Museum built one from his plans in 1991 and it worked.
Computing before the personal computer.Lovelace's program notes: Ada Lovelace's famous Note G laid out an algorithm for Bernoulli numbers, often called the first computer program, for an unbuilt machine.
Computing before the personal computer.Hollerith census tabulator: Herman Hollerith's punched-card machines counted the 1890 US census far faster than hand-tallying, and his firm later became part of IBM.
Computing before the personal computer.Turing's machine paper: His paper 'On Computable Numbers' described an imaginary machine able to run any algorithm, still the basis of what 'computable' means.
Computing before the personal computer.Zuse Z3: Konrad Zuse's Z3 in Berlin is widely seen as the first working programmable digital computer; Allied bombing destroyed it in 1943.
Computing before the personal computer.Harvard Mark I: About 16 metres long, this electromechanical giant was built with IBM for Howard Aiken, and Grace Hopper was one of its first programmers.
Computing before the personal computer.Hamming code: Richard Hamming devised it after weekend jobs kept crashing on single errors; it lets a computer detect and fix flipped bits itself.
Computing before the personal computer.A-0 compiler: Grace Hopper's A-0 system turned symbolic code into machine code, an early ancestor of the compilers programmers use today.
Computing before the personal computer.IBM RAMAC hard disk: The first commercial hard drive stored about 5 million characters on fifty 24-inch platters, and the whole cabinet weighed around a tonne.

How often you should replace these.Daily contact lens: Thrown away every night to avoid protein build-up that can cause eye infections.
How often you should replace these.Disposable razor: Shaving blades dull quickly, and a dull one tugs and nicks the skin more than a fresh blade.
How often you should replace these.Monthly contact lens: They need nightly cleaning, and sleeping in them raises the risk of serious eye infection.
How often you should replace these.Toothbrush: Dental associations recommend swapping it about every three months, or sooner when the bristles fray.
How often you should replace these.Bed pillow: Pillows collect skin flakes and dust mites; if one does not spring back after folding, it is probably time for a new one.
How often you should replace these.Car battery: A lead-acid battery usually lasts 3 to 5 years, and cold weather is when a weak one tends to fail.
How often you should replace these.Carbon monoxide alarm: It uses a sensor that wears out, and carbon monoxide is an odourless gas that is deadly yet undetectable without an alarm.
How often you should replace these.Smoke alarm: Even a working one should be replaced about every ten years, as its sensors lose sensitivity with age.
How often you should replace these.Asphalt shingle roof: Heat and UV slowly dry them out, and a good sign of an ageing roof is granules collecting in the gutters.
How often you should replace these.Copper water pipes: Copper plumbing is ancient: pipes in an Egyptian temple of around 2500 BC were made from it.

Japanese history: when these began.Jōmon period: Named for the cord-marked pottery, jōmon means cord pattern; these hunter-gatherers made some of the world's oldest pottery.
Japanese history: when these began.Yayoi period: Rice farming and metalworking arrived from the mainland; it is named for the Tokyo district where its pottery was first found.
Japanese history: when these began.Kofun period: It takes its name from huge keyhole-shaped burial mounds; the Daisen Kofun near Osaka is among the largest tombs in the world.
Japanese history: when these began.Asuka period: Buddhism's official arrival and Prince Shōtoku's reforms mark this age, which is named for the area where capitals were then located.
Japanese history: when these began.Nara period: Japan's first permanent capital, Heijō-kyō, was modeled on Tang China's Chang'an, and the Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji was built here.
Japanese history: when these began.Heian period: The capital moved to Heian-kyō, now Kyoto, and Murasaki Shikibu wrote The Tale of Genji, often called the world's first novel.
Japanese history: when these began.Kamakura shogunate: Minamoto no Yoritomo founded the first shogunate, shifting real power from the emperor to the warrior class for centuries.
Japanese history: when these began.First Mongol invasion: Kublai Khan's fleet attacked Japan; in 1281 a second try was wrecked by a typhoon later called kamikaze, the divine wind.
Japanese history: when these began.Muromachi period: Ashikaga shoguns ruled from Kyoto's Muromachi district, and the era saw Noh theater, the tea ceremony and Zen gardens flourish.
Japanese history: when these began.Sengoku (Warring States): A century of civil war among rival daimyo ended when Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu successively reunified Japan.

Calculating devices through history.Napier's bones: John Napier, who also invented logarithms, made rods that let you multiply by lining up digits.
Calculating devices through history.Slide rule: William Oughtred built it using logarithms; engineers used it for centuries, and the Apollo astronauts carried one.
Calculating devices through history.Pascaline: Blaise Pascal built it at about 19 to help his tax-collector father, and it added and subtracted with gears.
Calculating devices through history.Leibniz's stepped reckoner: It could multiply and divide by repeated addition using a stepped drum, though its carry mechanism was unreliable.
Calculating devices through history.Curta: Shaped like a pepper grinder, this pocket mechanical calculator was invented by Curt Herzstark, partly while held in Buchenwald.
Calculating devices through history.ANITA desktop calculator: The first all-electronic desktop calculator, from Britain's Bell Punch, used vacuum tubes rather than transistors.
Calculating devices through history.HP-35: The first scientific pocket calculator was reportedly sized to fit Bill Hewlett's shirt pocket, and it cost $395.
Calculating devices through history.HP-12C: This financial calculator is still sold more than forty years on, and uses reverse Polish notation.
Calculating devices through history.TI-83: A classroom staple whose users famously programmed games on it during class.
Calculating devices through history.TI-Nspire: Some versions can solve algebra symbolically, which is why many exams restrict them.

Milestones of early astronomy.Newgrange tomb aligned: Its passage floods with sunlight at winter solstice sunrise through a roof box, and it is older than Stonehenge and the pyramids.
Milestones of early astronomy.Stonehenge (main stones): The main stones align with the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset.
Milestones of early astronomy.Nebra sky disc: A bronze disc with gold symbols for the Sun, Moon and Pleiades, found in Germany by looters in 1999, is the oldest known depiction of the cosmos.
Milestones of early astronomy.Eratosthenes sizes the Earth: Using shadows at Syene and Alexandria, he estimated Earth's circumference to within a few percent, perhaps.
Milestones of early astronomy.Ptolemy's Almagest: Ptolemy's work set out an Earth-centered cosmos that dominated for 1,400 years; its name comes from the Arabic al-majisti.
Milestones of early astronomy.Al-Sufi's Book of Fixed Stars: The Persian astronomer described the Andromeda Galaxy as a little cloud, the earliest known record of it.
Milestones of early astronomy.Ulugh Beg's observatory: The Timurid ruler of Samarkand built a huge sextant and catalogued about a thousand stars, and was later assassinated.
Milestones of early astronomy.Tycho's Uraniborg: Tycho Brahe's island observatory on Hven, funded by the Danish king, produced the most precise naked-eye measurements ever made.
Milestones of early astronomy.Royal Observatory Greenwich: Founded by Charles II to improve navigation, it later hosted the prime meridian, set in 1884.
Milestones of early astronomy.Jantar Mantar, Jaipur: Sawai Jai Singh II built giant stone instruments here, including the Samrat Yantra, the world's largest stone sundial.

Aircraft and space companies, by foundin.Lockheed: The Loughead brothers changed the spelling so it matched how the name was pronounced.
Aircraft and space companies, by foundin.Boeing: Founded in Seattle by a timber magnate who began by building seaplanes.
Aircraft and space companies, by foundin.Douglas Aircraft: Its 1935 DC-3 transformed air travel, and the firm later merged into McDonnell Douglas and then Boeing.
Aircraft and space companies, by foundin.Cessna: Based in Wichita, Kansas, it built the 172, the most-produced aircraft in history.
Aircraft and space companies, by foundin.Bombardier: It began as a Quebec snowmobile maker before expanding into trains and aircraft, later adding Learjet and Canadair.
Aircraft and space companies, by foundin.Embraer: This Brazilian company, started as a government project, became the world's third-largest commercial aircraft maker.
Aircraft and space companies, by foundin.Airbus: Formed by European governments to rival American makers, it builds the A380, the largest passenger jet.
Aircraft and space companies, by foundin.Blue Origin: Founded by Jeff Bezos, it names its rockets after pioneers: New Shepard for Alan Shepard and New Glenn for John Glenn.
Aircraft and space companies, by foundin.SpaceX: Founded by Elon Musk, it landed an orbital-class rocket booster upright for the first time in 2015.
Aircraft and space companies, by foundin.Virgin Galactic: Founded by Richard Branson, it flies tourists on suborbital hops launched from a carrier plane above New Mexico.

Sports by the clock.NBA three-second lane rule: Offensive players can't loiter in the key for over three seconds, a rule meant to stop big men camping under the basket.
Sports by the clock.Time to inbound the ball: A closely guarded player holding the ball faces the same five-second limit before losing possession.
Sports by the clock.Time to cross half-court: FIBA allows 10 seconds, but the NBA shortened its backcourt limit to eight in 2001.
Sports by the clock.MLB pitch clock, bases empty: Introduced in 2023, it cut the average length of games by roughly 25 minutes.
Sports by the clock.NBA shot clock: Danny Biasone proposed it in 1954, working it out from the average number of shots per game he wanted.
Sports by the clock.Tennis serve clock: Grand Slams adopted a 25-second serve clock around 2018 and 2019 to speed up play between points.
Sports by the clock.NFL play clock: It starts when the previous play ends, and the league uses a shorter clock after certain stoppages.
Sports by the clock.Boxing rest between rounds: The rest gives the corner time to patch cuts, hand out water and offer advice.
Sports by the clock.Golf lost ball search: Under the Rules of Golf, a ball is considered lost after three minutes of searching, cut from five in 2019.
Sports by the clock.Soccer half-time: Matches are two 45-minute halves, and the break can last up to 15 minutes.

How loud these sounds are.Normal breathing: In a very quiet anechoic chamber, where sound is nearly absorbed, people report hearing their own breathing and heartbeat.
How loud these sounds are.Rustling leaves: The decibel scale is logarithmic: every 10 dB means ten times the sound energy, though it only sounds about twice as loud to us.
How loud these sounds are.Whisper: When you whisper, your vocal cords don't vibrate, and the sound is just breathy air through your mouth, which is why it sounds hissy.
How loud these sounds are.Refrigerator hum: That steady hum comes from the compressor and fan, and it's around the level of a quiet library.
How loud these sounds are.Normal conversation: Conversation sits at about 60 dB. Hearing experts say that continuous noise above about 85 dB can damage hearing over time.
How loud these sounds are.Vacuum cleaner: At around 75 dB, a vacuum is loud enough to drown out normal talk, though it's still below the level where damage starts for short exposures.
How loud these sounds are.Lawn mower: Health agencies suggest hearing protection for mowing if you do it for more than about two hours at this level.
How loud these sounds are.Chainsaw: Chainsaws are about 110 dB, a level at which unprotected ears can start to be harmed within just a couple of minutes.
How loud these sounds are.Ambulance siren: Sirens are designed to cut through traffic noise, and at close range at about 120 dB are near the threshold of pain.
How loud these sounds are.Jet takeoff, nearby: Standing near a jet taking off can reach about 140 dB, a level at which a single exposure can cause permanent hearing damage.

Record-breaking heights.Miracle Milly, smallest dog: This Puerto Rican Chihuahua, 9.65 cm tall, was crowned the world's smallest living dog by Guinness in 2013 and weighed about as much as a hardcover book.
Record-breaking heights.Thumbelina, smallest horse: This dwarf miniature horse from South Carolina was only 43 cm tall and about 26 pounds as an adult, and was the world's smallest horse ever recorded.
Record-breaking heights.Chandra Bahadur Dangi: The Nepalese man, measured at 54.6 cm in 2012, was recognized by Guinness as the shortest adult man in recorded history.
Record-breaking heights.Jyoti Amge: This Indian actress, measured at 62.8 cm, is the shortest living woman, and appeared in the TV series American Horror Story.
Record-breaking heights.Zeus, tallest dog: The Great Dane from Michigan, 111.8 cm at the shoulder, was named the world's tallest dog in 2011, and he lived until 2014.
Record-breaking heights.Big Jake, tallest horse: A Belgian draft horse from Wisconsin, about 210 cm at the shoulder, held the title of world's tallest horse until his death in 2021.
Record-breaking heights.Sultan Kösen: The Turkish farmer's height is 251 cm, and he also has the world's largest hands, with the longest measuring about 28.5 cm.
Record-breaking heights.Robert Wadlow: The man from Alton, Illinois, reached 272 cm, the tallest person ever verified, and he was still growing when he died at age 22 in 1940.
Record-breaking heights.Record sunflower: Grown in Germany in 2014, this sunflower reached 9.17 m, taller than a two-story house, which is a record for the tallest sunflower.
Record-breaking heights.Record snowwoman (Maine): Built in Bethel, Maine, in 2008, this snow sculpture was named Olympia Snowe, after a US senator from the state, and had a 37-meter height.

Fictional detectives, by debut year.C. Auguste Dupin: Poe's Parisian sleuth in the 1841 Rue Morgue story is often called the first detective of modern fiction.
Fictional detectives, by debut year.Sherlock Holmes: Conan Doyle's detective debuted in A Study in Scarlet, and he's based partly on a real Edinburgh surgeon.
Fictional detectives, by debut year.Father Brown: The priest-detective by G. K. Chesterton solves crimes by understanding people, not by clues alone.
Fictional detectives, by debut year.Hercule Poirot: Agatha Christie's Belgian detective debuted in The Mysterious Affair at Styles, and he gets a New York Times obituary when he dies.
Fictional detectives, by debut year.Lord Peter Wimsey: Dorothy L. Sayers's aristocratic detective debuted in Whose Body?, and he suffers from shell shock from the Great War.
Fictional detectives, by debut year.Nancy Drew: The teen detective drives a blue roadster in the series, and she has been a ghostwritten character from the start.
Fictional detectives, by debut year.Philip Marlowe: Raymond Chandler's private eye debuted in The Big Sleep, and his hard-boiled voice shaped noir.
Fictional detectives, by debut year.Inspector Morse: Colin Dexter's inspector loves opera and crosswords, and he's the lead in a long-running TV series.
Fictional detectives, by debut year.Jack Reacher: Lee Child's drifter ex-military investigator debuted in Killing Floor, and he travels with little more than a toothbrush.
Fictional detectives, by debut year.Lisbeth Salander: Stieg Larsson's hacker heroine debuted in The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo, and she has a famous dragon tattoo.

How high humans have gone.La Rinconada, highest town: La Rinconada in Peru is often called the highest permanent settlement, and it's a gold mining town in the Andes.
How high humans have gone.Summit of Everest: Everest's summit is 8,849 m, and the summit stays high, with the air containing only about a third of the oxygen at sea level.
How high humans have gone.Airliner at cruise: Airliners fly high to use thinner air, and passengers see the curvature of the Earth only faintly.
How high humans have gone.Concorde at cruise: Concorde flew at about twice the speed of sound, and its windows were small because of the high altitude.
How high humans have gone.Kittinger's 1960 jump: In 1960, Joseph Kittinger leapt from a balloon at over 31 km, and he reached near the speed of sound.
How high humans have gone.Alan Eustace's 2014 jump: In 2014, Google executive Alan Eustace jumped from a balloon in a custom suit, breaking Kittinger's record.
How high humans have gone.International Space Station: The ISS orbits about 400 km up, and it has been continuously occupied since 2000.
How high humans have gone.Gemini 11's high orbit: In 1966, Gemini 11 boosted itself to a record orbital altitude, and it was a record for humans for a long time.
How high humans have gone.Apollo astronauts on the Moon: Twelve Apollo astronauts walked on the Moon, and the Moon is on average about 384,000 km away.
How high humans have gone.Apollo 13 behind the Moon: Apollo 13's crew were farther from Earth than any humans before, and they set the distance record on their emergency loop.

Old Testament history books, in Bible or.Leviticus: It contains the command to 'love your neighbour as yourself', best known from Jesus's later quoting of it.
Old Testament history books, in Bible or.Numbers: The name comes from two censuses of the Israelites that it records, and its Hebrew title means 'in the wilderness'.
Old Testament history books, in Bible or.Deuteronomy: The title means 'second law' in Greek, and the book is largely Moses's final speeches before his death.
Old Testament history books, in Bible or.Joshua: It describes the fall of Jericho's walls, and opens the group of books Jewish tradition calls the Former Prophets.
Old Testament history books, in Bible or.Judges: It tells of Deborah, Gideon and Samson, in a time with no king, when 'everyone did what was right in their own eyes'.
Old Testament history books, in Bible or.Ruth: One of only two books named for women, the other being Esther, it ends with an ancestor of King David.
Old Testament history books, in Bible or.1 Samuel: It includes the tale of David and Goliath, and the prophet Samuel anointing Israel's first king, Saul.
Old Testament history books, in Bible or.2 Samuel: The two books of Samuel were originally one scroll, split into two only when translated into Greek.
Old Testament history books, in Bible or.1 Kings: It describes Solomon building the Temple in Jerusalem, and the visit of the Queen of Sheba.
Old Testament history books, in Bible or.2 Kings: It closes with Jerusalem's fall to Babylon in 586 BC, and includes the prophet Elijah's ride to heaven in a fiery chariot.

Impact craters on Earth by age.Kaali (Estonia): A group of nine craters on Estonia's Saaremaa island, the largest holding a lake about 110 m across.
Impact craters on Earth by age.Meteor Crater (Arizona): About 1.2 km wide, it was used by Apollo astronauts to train for the Moon.
Impact craters on Earth by age.Wolfe Creek (Australia): This 875 m crater in Western Australia's desert gave its name to a horror film.
Impact craters on Earth by age.Ries (Germany): In Bavaria, the town of Nördlingen sits inside it, and its church is built from impact-formed rock.
Impact craters on Earth by age.Popigai (Siberia): Its crater in Siberia is about 100 km across and contains impact diamonds.
Impact craters on Earth by age.Chicxulub (Mexico): Linked to the dinosaurs' extinction, it lies buried beneath Mexico's Yucatán, partly offshore.
Impact craters on Earth by age.Manicouagan (Canada): A ring-shaped lake in Quebec that is visible from space, nicknamed the Eye of Quebec.
Impact craters on Earth by age.Siljan (Sweden): One of Europe's largest impact structures, in Sweden's Dalarna region.
Impact craters on Earth by age.Sudbury (Canada): The impact left rich nickel and copper ore, and the Ontario city has a giant nickel coin statue.
Impact craters on Earth by age.Vredefort (South Africa): The largest verified impact structure on Earth, it was originally around 300 km wide.

Literary prizes, by year first awarded.Nobel Prize in Literature: The first winner was French poet Sully Prudhomme in 1901, and Tolstoy never won it.
Literary prizes, by year first awarded.Prix Goncourt: The prize money is a symbolic ten euros, but winning means sales that can reach hundreds of thousands of copies.
Literary prizes, by year first awarded.Pulitzer Prize: Funded by publisher Joseph Pulitzer's will, it began in 1917 and now covers letters, drama and music as well as journalism.
Literary prizes, by year first awarded.Newbery Medal: It honours a US children's book author each year and is named for John Newbery, an 18th-century English publisher.
Literary prizes, by year first awarded.Caldecott Medal: It honours picture book illustration and is named for the English illustrator Randolph Caldecott.
Literary prizes, by year first awarded.Edgar Award: Named for Edgar Allan Poe, it honours mystery writing, and winners receive a small porcelain bust of him.
Literary prizes, by year first awarded.Hugo Award: Named for Hugo Gernsback, who coined the term scientific fiction, its trophy is a shiny silver rocket.
Literary prizes, by year first awarded.Nebula Award: Voted on by working science fiction and fantasy writers, it is awarded by their own association.
Literary prizes, by year first awarded.Booker Prize: Once restricted to the Commonwealth, since 2014 any English-language novel published in the UK or Ireland can win.
Literary prizes, by year first awarded.Women's Prize for Fiction: It was founded in 1996 after an all-male Booker shortlist in 1991 prompted a campaign for a prize celebrating women writers.

Movie musicals by release.The Wizard of Oz: Over the Rainbow was nearly cut from the film for slowing the pace, and the picture was shot in glorious Technicolor.
Movie musicals by release.Singin' in the Rain: Gene Kelly reportedly danced the title number with a fever of about 39 °C, in a studio rain tank.
Movie musicals by release.West Side Story (original): The original won 10 Academy Awards, a record for a musical, and moved Romeo and Juliet to New York street gangs.
Movie musicals by release.Mary Poppins: It won five Oscars, including best actress for Julie Andrews; Walt Disney spent about 20 years winning the rights from author P. L. Travers.
Movie musicals by release.The Sound of Music: It is based on the real von Trapp family who fled Austria, and it briefly became the highest-grossing film of all time.
Movie musicals by release.Grease: Grease was one of the biggest hits of 1978, and the film added new songs, including You're the One That I Want.
Movie musicals by release.Chicago: Chicago was the first musical to win best picture since Oliver! in 1968, with Catherine Zeta-Jones winning supporting actress.
Movie musicals by release.Mamma Mia!: Built around ABBA's hits, Mamma Mia! was mostly filmed on Greek islands, with a chapel on Skopelos as its wedding scene.
Movie musicals by release.La La Land: It tied the record with 14 Oscar nominations and was famously, mistakenly, announced as best picture before the error was corrected.
Movie musicals by release.The Greatest Showman: Inspired by showman P. T. Barnum, its soundtrack became one of the best-selling albums of its time, topping the UK charts for weeks.

Grammar and style guides, by first editi.Lowth's English Grammar: Bishop Robert Lowth's book helped popularize rules such as not ending a sentence with a preposition, which Latin never needed.
Grammar and style guides, by first editi.Murray's English Grammar: Lindley Murray's textbook, written in New York, was a bestseller across the English-speaking world for decades.
Grammar and style guides, by first editi.Hart's Rules: Printed for Oxford University Press by Horace Hart, it began as a guide for the press's own compositors.
Grammar and style guides, by first editi.Chicago Manual of Style: The 'CMOS' from the University of Chicago Press is now in its 18th edition.
Grammar and style guides, by first editi.Strunk's Elements of Style: Strunk's little book, self-published at Cornell, was later revised by E. B. White. Its famous advice is 'Omit needless words'.
Grammar and style guides, by first editi.Fowler's Modern English Usage: H. W. Fowler's witty usage guide helped define 'correct' English for generations.
Grammar and style guides, by first editi.Gowers' Plain Words: Sir Ernest Gowers was asked to write it to help British civil servants write more clearly.
Grammar and style guides, by first editi.AP Stylebook: Newsrooms across America follow it. It began in 1953 as a short stylesheet for AP journalists.
Grammar and style guides, by first editi.MLA Handbook: The Modern Language Association's handbook set the standard for citing sources in humanities papers.
Grammar and style guides, by first editi.Eats, Shoots & Leaves: Lynne Truss's bestseller takes its title from a joke about a panda and a misplaced comma.

Egyptian rulers, by when they reigned.Narmer: Often credited with uniting Upper and Lower Egypt. A famous carved palette shows him wearing both crowns.
Egyptian rulers, by when they reigned.Djoser: His Step Pyramid at Saqqara, designed by Imhotep, is the earliest large stone building in the world.
Egyptian rulers, by when they reigned.Khufu: He built the Great Pyramid at Giza, which stayed the tallest human-made structure for around 3,800 years.
Egyptian rulers, by when they reigned.Hatshepsut: A woman who ruled as king, she is shown in statues with the pharaoh's false beard.
Egyptian rulers, by when they reigned.Akhenaten: He promoted the worship of a single sun-disc god, Aten, and was the husband of Nefertiti.
Egyptian rulers, by when they reigned.Tutankhamun: He died young, about nineteen, and his tomb was found almost intact in 1922.
Egyptian rulers, by when they reigned.Ramesses II: Ruled for about 66 years, built Abu Simbel and signed an early peace treaty with the Hittites.
Egyptian rulers, by when they reigned.Psamtik I: He freed Egypt from Assyrian rule and founded the 26th Dynasty, using Greek mercenaries.
Egyptian rulers, by when they reigned.Ptolemy I: A general of Alexander the Great who founded the dynasty that ruled Egypt until Cleopatra.
Egyptian rulers, by when they reigned.Cleopatra VII: She lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.

Railway milestones through history.Stockton & Darlington Railway: Opened in northern England, it was the first public railway to use steam locomotives, built by George Stephenson.
Railway milestones through history.Liverpool & Manchester Rly: The first intercity railway powered entirely by steam. William Huskisson, an MP, was killed on opening day.
Railway milestones through history.London Underground opens: The world's first underground railway ran steam locomotives through gas-lit tunnels.
Railway milestones through history.US transcontinental railroad: Completed with a golden spike at Promontory Summit, Utah, linking the coasts by rail.
Railway milestones through history.Orient Express first run: Ran Paris to Istanbul in luxury, and later inspired Agatha Christie's Murder on the Orient Express.
Railway milestones through history.Paris Métro opens: Its Art Nouveau station entrances were designed by Hector Guimard.
Railway milestones through history.New York City Subway opens: Opened on 27 October 1904. The system runs around the clock.
Railway milestones through history.Shinkansen bullet train: Opened days before the Tokyo Olympics, and has had no passenger deaths from accidents.
Railway milestones through history.TGV enters service: A French train that set the conventional-rail speed record of 574.8 km/h in 2007.
Railway milestones through history.Eurostar enters service: It connected London, Paris and Brussels through the Channel Tunnel.

When these social networks launched.SixDegrees: Launched in 1997, this is often called the first social network, and it let users list friends and send messages.
When these social networks launched.Friendster: Founded in California, it was one of the first big social networks, reaching millions before Facebook overtook it.
When these social networks launched.LinkedIn: Founded by Reid Hoffman and others, it was bought by Microsoft in 2016, and it focuses on professional networking.
When these social networks launched.Reddit: Its mascot is an alien called Snoo, and the name comes from a pun on 'I read it'.
When these social networks launched.Tumblr: It's a blogging platform that Yahoo! bought in 2013, and then Verizon sold on to Automattic.
When these social networks launched.WhatsApp: The messaging app that Facebook bought in 2014, and its founders were former Yahoo employees.
When these social networks launched.Pinterest: This visual platform, where users 'pin' ideas to boards, started as a place for collecting images.
When these social networks launched.Discord: Originally built for gamers, it grew into a chat platform for communities, with servers and voice channels.
When these social networks launched.Clubhouse: This invitation-only audio app boomed during the pandemic, with celebrities and tech figures in rooms.
When these social networks launched.Threads: Meta's text-based rival to X, it signed up 100 million users in about five days after its launch.

First year these awards were handed out.Nobel Prize: Funded by the fortune of dynamite inventor Alfred Nobel, it was first awarded in 1901, and the economics prize was added much later.
First year these awards were handed out.Pulitzer Prize: Journalism, letters and music honors created through publisher Joseph Pulitzer's bequest, first given in 1917.
First year these awards were handed out.Academy Awards: The first ceremony in 1929 was a private dinner lasting about 15 minutes, and winners were announced months ahead.
First year these awards were handed out.Fields Medal: Mathematics has no Nobel, so this medal, given every four years to those under 40, is its closest equivalent.
First year these awards were handed out.Tony Awards: Named after actress and director Antoinette Perry, it honors Broadway, and its first ceremony was held in 1947.
First year these awards were handed out.Emmy Awards: Its name is a feminized version of "immy", slang for the image orthicon camera tube used in early TV.
First year these awards were handed out.Ballon d'Or: The "Golden Ball" is awarded by France Football magazine, and its first winner was English winger Stanley Matthews.
First year these awards were handed out.Grammy Awards: Named for the gramophone, the trophy is a small golden gramophone, and the first ceremony was in 1959.
First year these awards were handed out.Booker Prize: The UK's top fiction award, first won by P. H. Newby, which has since gone to authors like Salman Rushdie and Hilary Mantel.
First year these awards were handed out.Turner Prize: Named for the painter J. M. W. Turner, this art prize is known for controversy, such as Tracey Emin's unmade bed in 1999.

A bite's journey through the digestive t.Mouth: Your tongue and teeth begin breaking food down here, and saliva starts digesting starch with an enzyme called amylase.
A bite's journey through the digestive t.Pharynx: This crossroads of the throat shared by air and food has a flap called the epiglottis to keep food out of your windpipe.
A bite's journey through the digestive t.Esophagus: This muscular tube squeezes food downward in waves called peristalsis, so you can even swallow while hanging upside down.
A bite's journey through the digestive t.Stomach: Stomach acid is strong enough to dissolve metal, so the stomach protects itself by renewing its mucus lining every few days.
A bite's journey through the digestive t.Duodenum: This first section of the small intestine is only about 25 cm long, but it receives bile and pancreatic juices to break down food.
A bite's journey through the digestive t.Jejunum: The jejunum has many finger-like folds that absorb most of your sugars and amino acids from the food passing through.
A bite's journey through the digestive t.Ileum: The ileum absorbs vitamin B12 and bile salts, ending the small intestine, which in total is about six meters long.
A bite's journey through the digestive t.Cecum: This pouch starts the large intestine, and the appendix hangs from it, possibly serving as a reserve for helpful gut bacteria.
A bite's journey through the digestive t.Colon: The colon absorbs water and houses trillions of bacteria, which make vitamins like K and help ferment fiber we cannot digest.
A bite's journey through the digestive t.Rectum: The final stretch of the large intestine holds waste until you are ready to go, and stretch receptors tell your brain it's time.

Lengths of sporting gear.Table tennis paddle: Table tennis paddle sizes are not regulated, but the blade must be at least 85 percent natural wood.
Lengths of sporting gear.Badminton racket: A smash can send a shuttlecock past 400 km/h, the fastest of any racket sport.
Lengths of sporting gear.Tennis racket: Its maximum is 29 inches; graphite frames replaced wood in the 1980s.
Lengths of sporting gear.Cricket bat: Maximum is 38 inches, and it is made from willow.
Lengths of sporting gear.Baseball bat: Major League rules limit bats to 42 inches and require wood: ash, maple or birch.
Lengths of sporting gear.Golf club: Rules cap clubs, other than putters, at 48 inches long.
Lengths of sporting gear.Ice hockey stick: Sticks are cut to the player's height, and a curved blade helps with shooting.
Lengths of sporting gear.Men's javelin: Jan Zelezny's 1996 throw of 98.48 m is still the record.
Lengths of sporting gear.Rowing sweep oar: A sweep oar is held in both hands with one per rower, unlike sculls where each rower uses two shorter oars.
Lengths of sporting gear.Pole vault pole: Flexible fiberglass or carbon poles let vaulters clear heights over six meters.

Metals by density.Lithium: Lithium is the lightest metal and floats on water. It's now vital for rechargeable batteries in phones and electric cars.
Metals by density.Sodium: Sodium is soft enough to cut with a knife and reacts violently with water, and it floats too.
Metals by density.Magnesium: Magnesium burns with a dazzling white light, and it was used in early camera flashes.
Metals by density.Aluminium: Aluminium was once costlier than gold, and Napoleon III reportedly served honored guests with aluminium cutlery.
Metals by density.Titanium: Titanium is as strong as many steels but much lighter, and it's very resistant to corrosion, so it's used in jets and implants.
Metals by density.Copper: Copper conducts electricity extremely well, and it's among the first metals humans worked, over 10,000 years ago.
Metals by density.Silver: Silver is the best electrical conductor of all the metals, even better than copper, but it costs far more.
Metals by density.Mercury: Mercury is the only metal that's liquid at room temperature, and it's so dense that iron floats on it.
Metals by density.Gold: Gold is so malleable that a single gram can be beaten into a sheet about a square meter in size.
Metals by density.Osmium: Osmium is the densest naturally occurring element, and a block of it the size of a sugar cube would weigh about 22 grams.

How well these conduct heat.Air: Air is a poor conductor, which is why double-glazed windows and fluffy insulation work by trapping it.
How well these conduct heat.Pine wood: Pine wood conducts heat slowly, which is why wooden spoons stay cool in a hot pot.
How well these conduct heat.Water: Water conducts heat poorly compared with metals, but it holds heat very well, so it takes a long time to warm up.
How well these conduct heat.Window glass: Window glass conducts heat much better than air, so single-pane windows lose a lot of heat.
How well these conduct heat.Ice: Ice conducts heat about four times better than water, and it's why a frozen pond chills the air above it quickly.
How well these conduct heat.Stainless steel: Stainless steel is a surprisingly poor conductor for a metal, which is why steel pots often have copper or aluminium bases.
How well these conduct heat.Cast iron: Cast iron heats slowly and unevenly, but once hot it holds the heat for a long time, which is great for searing.
How well these conduct heat.Aluminium: Aluminium is lightweight and conducts heat well, which is why it's used in heat sinks and cooking pans.
How well these conduct heat.Copper: Copper is prized in cookware because it spreads heat quickly and evenly, and the best pans have copper cores.
How well these conduct heat.Diamond: Diamond conducts heat better than any metal, and that's why a diamond feels cold to the touch, and why it's used as a heat spreader in electronics.

When these PlayStation hits first came o.Crash Bandicoot: Naughty Dog's marsupial hero was Sony's answer to Mario on the original PlayStation.
When these PlayStation hits first came o.Gran Turismo: Kazunori Yamauchi's driving simulator took five years to make and sold over ten million copies.
When these PlayStation hits first came o.Spyro the Dragon: Made by Insomniac Games, whose later hit was Ratchet and Clank, about a purple dragon.
When these PlayStation hits first came o.Ratchet and Clank: A Lombax and his robot sidekick from Insomniac Games, an early PS2 hit with a huge arsenal.
When these PlayStation hits first came o.Uncharted: Naughty Dog's treasure hunter Nathan Drake brought a cinematic, Indiana Jones-like style to the PlayStation 3.
When these PlayStation hits first came o.LittleBigPlanet: Sackboy's 'Play, Create, Share' game let players build and share their own levels.
When these PlayStation hits first came o.The Last of Us: Naughty Dog's tale of survivors in a world ruined by a fungus. It was adapted into an HBO series in 2023.
When these PlayStation hits first came o.Horizon Zero Dawn: Guerrilla Games, known for shooters, made this open-world about Aloy hunting robot dinosaurs.
When these PlayStation hits first came o.Ghost of Tsushima: Sucker Punch's samurai game is set during the Mongol invasion of 1274. Wind is used as a guide for players.
When these PlayStation hits first came o.Astro Bot: Won Game of the Year at 2024's The Game Awards, a rare feat for a platformer.

Stars by surface temperature.Proxima Centauri: The nearest known star to the Sun, a red dwarf about 4.2 light years away, invisible to the naked eye.
Stars by surface temperature.Betelgeuse: A red supergiant in Orion's shoulder that dimmed noticeably in 2019 and 2020.
Stars by surface temperature.Aldebaran: An orange giant, the eye of Taurus. Its Arabic name means 'the follower'.
Stars by surface temperature.Arcturus: The brightest star in the northern celestial hemisphere. Its light opened the 1933 Chicago World's Fair.
Stars by surface temperature.The Sun: Often called a yellow dwarf, though it is really white. Its core is around 15 million kelvins.
Stars by surface temperature.Procyon: A bright star in Canis Minor with a white dwarf companion.
Stars by surface temperature.Sirius: The brightest star in the night sky, about 8.6 light years away. It is nicknamed the Dog Star.
Stars by surface temperature.Rigel: A blue supergiant in Orion's foot, over 100,000 times more luminous than the Sun.
Stars by surface temperature.Spica: A close pair of stars in Virgo. Hipparchus used it to discover Earth's precession.
Stars by surface temperature.Zeta Puppis: Also called Naos, among the hottest naked-eye stars, though it lies in the southern sky.

Burger chains, by founding year.White Castle: White Castle's small square sliders helped make hamburgers respectable in America after a bad reputation in the early 1900s. It's often called the first burger chain.
Carl Karcher started with a single hot dog cart in Los Angeles. His chain grew into a Western burger giant.
Burger chains, by founding year.In-N-Out Burger: This California chain keeps a short menu and uses fresh, never frozen, beef. Its not-quite-secret menu includes "Animal Style" burgers.
Burger chains, by founding year.Whataburger: This Texas chain started in Corpus Christi, and its orange-and-white A-frame roofs are iconic. It once offered a burger so big it needed a fork.
Burger chains, by founding year.Jack in the Box: Based in San Diego, it was among the first chains to use a two-way speaker box at the drive-thru. The name comes from its clown-faced box.
Burger chains, by founding year.Sonic: Founded as a drive-in in Oklahoma, this chain is known for roller-skating carhops. Its menu includes slushes in hundreds of combinations.
Burger chains, by founding year.Hardee's: Hardee's began in Greenville, North Carolina, and is known for hand-breaded biscuits at breakfast. Its Thickburgers helped make big burgers a menu staple.
Burger chains, by founding year.Wendy's: Dave Thomas named it for his daughter, whose nickname was Wendy. Its square patties are meant to show that "quality has no corners."
Burger chains, by founding year.Culver's: Born in Wisconsin, this chain is known for its ButterBurgers and fresh frozen custard. Its restaurants are mostly franchised by locals.
Burger chains, by founding year.Smashburger: Founded in Denver, this chain is named for the technique of mashing a ball of beef onto a hot griddle. It creates a crusty edge.

Tarot Major Arcana, by card number.The Fool: Numbered zero, it begins the journey, and is believed to be the ancestor of the Joker in a playing deck.
Tarot Major Arcana, by card number.The Magician: The table before him holds symbols of all four suits, showing a mastery of every element at his disposal.
Tarot Major Arcana, by card number.The Empress: Associated with Venus, nature and abundance, she is usually seen wearing a crown of twelve stars.
Tarot Major Arcana, by card number.The Lovers: Often shows Adam and Eve beneath an angel, and the card is about choices rather than only romance.
Tarot Major Arcana, by card number.The Chariot: Pulled by two sphinxes, one black and one white, which stand for opposing forces under control.
Tarot Major Arcana, by card number.The Hermit: Carries a lantern in a symbol of inward search, showing a figure who has withdrawn to find wisdom.
Tarot Major Arcana, by card number.Death: It rarely means literal death; readers usually take it as transformation or an ending that makes room for something new.
Tarot Major Arcana, by card number.The Tower: Lightning strikes a tower and people fall, signaling sudden upheaval that destroys false foundations.
Tarot Major Arcana, by card number.The Moon: A dog and a wolf howl at the moon, with a crayfish rising from a pool, for the unconscious and the uncertain.
Tarot Major Arcana, by card number.The World: The final card of the major arcana, showing a dancer in a wreath, and it signals completion.

Great human firsts.Swim across the Channel: Captain Matthew Webb did it by breaststroke in 1875, taking over 21 hours.
Great human firsts.Reach the South Pole: Roald Amundsen got there first, about five weeks ahead of Scott.
Great human firsts.Solo nonstop Atlantic flight: Charles Lindbergh flew the Spirit of St. Louis from New York to Paris in about 33 hours, winning the $25,000 Orteig Prize.
Great human firsts.Summit Mount Everest: News of Hillary and Tenzing's success reached London on the morning of Elizabeth II's coronation.
Great human firsts.Run a sub-four-minute mile: Roger Bannister ran 3:59.4, but the record lasted just 46 days before John Landy broke it.
Great human firsts.Reach the Challenger Deep: Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh spent only about 20 minutes at the bottom, in the bathyscaphe Trieste.
Great human firsts.Orbit the Earth: Yuri Gagarin's flight lasted 108 minutes in Vostok 1.
Great human firsts.Run 100 m under 10 seconds: Jim Hines ran 9.95 at the Mexico City Olympics, helped by thin air.
Great human firsts.Walk on the Moon: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin spent about two and a half hours outside on the surface.
Great human firsts.Run a sub-two-hour marathon: Eliud Kipchoge ran 1:59:40 in Vienna, but it was not an official record because of rotating pacers.

A sea turtle's life, step by step.Mother crawls ashore at night: Females return to the beach where they hatched, sometimes after decades, to nest. They may navigate by the magnetic signature of their home shore.
A sea turtle's life, step by step.Digs a nest in the sand: She digs a flask-shaped hole with her back flippers. It can take her an hour or more, and she goes into a trance-like state while laying.
A sea turtle's life, step by step.Lays about 100 eggs: The soft, leathery eggs are the size of ping-pong balls. A turtle lays several clutches in a season, but few hatchlings will survive.
A sea turtle's life, step by step.Covers them up: She covers the nest and camouflages it by flinging sand around. Then she leaves, and never meets her young.
A sea turtle's life, step by step.Swims back to sea: Her tracks in the sand can be seen the next morning, as she makes her way back. She may not nest again for two or three years.
A sea turtle's life, step by step.Eggs warm for two months: The temperature of the sand decides the sex of the hatchlings. Warmer nests give mostly females, which worries scientists about climate change.
A sea turtle's life, step by step.Hatchlings dig out: The babies hatch at about the same time, and work together to dig up to the surface. They often wait until night to emerge.
A sea turtle's life, step by step.Race to the sea: Hatchlings find the sea by heading towards the brightest horizon, which is why artificial lights on beaches can mislead them. Predators catch many on the way.
A sea turtle's life, step by step.Drift for years at sea: Young turtles ride ocean currents for years in the so-called lost years, hiding among floating seaweed. Scientists know little about this time.
A sea turtle's life, step by step.Return to nest on that beach: After 20 to 30 years, they reach maturity, then return to the beach where they were born. Only about one in a thousand makes it.
